title: DoorDash Announces Pricing Principles
summary: DoorDash shares pricing principles and asks lawmakers to protect discounts that help consumers save and local businesses grow.
body_markdown:
Every day, we work to make DoorDash better — and that starts by offering consumers more selection and greater affordability. When we can offer consumers a better product at a lower price, we drive more sales and value for local businesses that are working to compete with the biggest ecommerce players, and we generate more earning opportunities for Dashers.


So when shopping for groceries, a favorite meal, or daily essentials on DoorDash, you deserve to know that we aren’t using your data to raise your price. **That’s surveillance pricing, and we don’t do it** .


Today, we’re sharing our pricing commitments, explaining how we support local businesses by investing in affordability, and calling on lawmakers to ban surveillance pricing while also protecting the deals that help people save money.


**DoorDash’s pricing commitments**


You can count on the following commitments when you come to DoorDash to shop:


-


**We do not personalize prices.** Prices on DoorDash are not personalized and are never based on protected characteristics like race, religion, gender, or age. Nor are they based on the type of phone a consumer uses (a misconception that is simply false).


-


**Same item, same store, same price.** Two consumers ordering from the same store at the same time see the same item price.


-


**We don’t engage in dynamic or real-time surge pricing.** Item prices and fees do not change in real-time based on spikes in demand. In bad weather, we may add a fee to help support Dasher pay and mitigate service disruptions. This fee is disclosed to consumers before checkout.


-


**Your order history is never used to raise prices.** If you order a lot of soda on DoorDash, we won’t increase the price of a 12-pack because we think you’ll pay more. In fact, we might offer you a discount on a new soda we think you’ll like.


-


**We will always show you every cent you’ll pay in fees and prices.** You will always see what you’re paying before you check out.


**Saving you money**


At a time when the cost of living is so important to so many people, the ability to save on groceries, a family dinner, or medicine and household essentials really matters. DoorDash and local businesses on our platform offer deals to attract new consumers and help generate more sales — which keeps more dollars flowing through local economies. We might offer a deal to a first-time consumer, or someone who hasn’t ordered on DoorDash in a while. The makers of a new brand of laundry detergent might offer a discount to a consumer who has ordered laundry detergent on DoorDash in the past. If a consumer has ordered a particular type of cuisine in the past, we may suggest other restaurants serving that type of cuisine and offer the consumer a deal to try them. These deals are for a limited time and based off the same list price that every consumer sees when ordering from the same store at the same time.


In 2025, consumers in the U.S. saved more than $12 billion from deals on the DoorDash Marketplace. People like a good deal, especially ones that are relevant to them. Promotions based on what you actually like are more useful than offering everyone the same discount, whether it’s meaningful to them or not. Personalized deals help make sure dog owners get deals on dog food and cat owners get deals on cat food.


**DoorDash supports banning surveillance pricing — and protecting deals that make life more affordable**


Lawmakers across the United States are moving to outlaw surveillance pricing, and they’re right to do so. Several U.S. states have already passed legislation, and we call on other policymakers to act.


As they do, they should draw a bright line between surveillance pricing and deals. Surveillance pricing aims to individualize list prices. A deal, like a coupon or discount, promotes affordability by lowering what you pay off a list price, and may be tailored to what you like.


We support banning surveillance pricing and will work with policymakers to ensure any legislation doesn’t unintentionally ban the deals that help people save money every day, like coupons, discounts, or loyalty programs. The test for any affordability agenda must be whether it helps lower prices, and banning deals clearly would not do that. We’re eager to work with lawmakers to make life more affordable, and we’re ready to get started.


**Q&A**


***Q. What is the difference between a price and a fee?***


The list price of an item is what it costs – that amount will never be raised on our platform based on who is making the purchase. A fee is the associated cost of getting that item to you, running our platform, and paying your Dasher. Fees may vary based on factors like the merchant you’re ordering from and the distance and effort it takes to get the order to you.


***Q. DoorDash fees can vary. Isn’t that dynamic pricing?***


No. When people talk about dynamic pricing, they usually mean changing the price of goods or services in real time or near-real time to respond to supply and demand signals. Our fees vary based on factors such as the delivery address and how much work it takes to fulfill your order; they don’t move up and down in real time depending on demand.


In extreme weather, consumers may see a separate Weather Impact Fee, which is based on demand and the number of available Dashers. But this fee does not vary based on the consumer placing the order and is meant to mitigate service disruptions.


***Q. Does DoorDash hold a patent to target consumers based on how ‘agitated’ they are?***


No. We do not use a consumer’s emotional state, stress level, or biometric data to affect the amount we charge them. We have no way to know how hungry you are, and being hungry doesn’t mean you’re shown higher item prices on DoorDash. Period.


Like many companies, we file patents on a wide range of concepts, and most never become products. In 2025, we applied for a patent to identify when a consumer is struggling with the app, such as not being able to complete an order or find Support.


This patent was misconstrued as something potentially nefarious, and while it was never our intent and the patent was never used, we withdrew the application entirely.


***Q. If you don’t support surveillance pricing, why do you disclose you use personal data in New York State?***


New York’s law has created some confusion. To complete a delivery, we need to know the delivery address and we use that address to estimate how long it will take to deliver the order and to determine the fees to charge. Because we use that information, New York requires a disclosure. Simply put, disclosure doesn't mean there is surveillance pricing or something inappropriate happening.
